score_note: Editorial rubric: 40% hook + 40% cliffhanger + 20% standalone clarity; ties broken by cliffhanger tension, hook strength, and punchier duration.

coverage.reason: The replacement bride declares the betrayal immediately; cut on the unanswered question, before the sister explains how long.
The rebuke is satisfying but resolves the humiliation emotionally; no equally strong unresolved cut with a clear opening survives the shortlist.
A woman is dragged from a church and a stranger challenges the guards; the cut withholds the fight and his identity.
The wedding acceptance and exit offer payoff; stronger marriage conflict appears in episode 45.
The ruined ledger is recovered and reassured over; the sacrifice premise in episode 12 gives a clearer open loop.
Domestic rebuilding is warm but has a slow opening and little unresolved urgency.
Gerald threatens the husband but then flees; a long version leaks the payoff and a short one needs more setup.
The beard mystery is gentle teasing; neither the opening nor the unresolved stakes compete with the shortlisted scenes.
The sick-child arc resolves; the late Duke rumor is promising but mostly exposition without a strong immediate hook.
Wound tending and romantic reassurance deliver intimacy rather than a distinct unresolved event.
The theft accusation supplies immediate stakes; his consent to the search commits the scene without showing the watch discovery.
A sister demands she crawl through frozen thorns with bare hands, then makes her husband's life the price of refusal.
The thorn search is visually painful and finds the ring; episode 12 sets up the same dilemma more clearly without its answer.
The ring is found and husband freed; the revenge vow is less specific than the already selected threats.
The confrontation escalates from refusal and assault to a three-against-one challenge; the fight remains unseen.
The fight and interrogation reveal who paid the thugs; episode 15 cuts before that payoff.
Tender domestic exchanges close with trust rather than an urgent unknown.
An urgent order to leave becomes a refusal to abandon her mother's book; cut on her scream before Alexander tackles her to safety.
The hidden Duke and imprisoned mother are interesting, but the informant scene relies on several unfamiliar names.
Villain succession talk and the healer's resolve need substantial context; other episodes make the poisoning threat explicit.
The emergency with Toby offers a possible alternative, but the rescue resolves and the late Duchess setup requires a second premise.
A warning about recognition establishes the disguise; her plan to save the Duchess carries her through the servants' entrance.
The accusation of poisoning is the hook; an approaching intruder interrupts her attempt to save the Duchess.
The assault is shocking, but punishment and a return vow have a weaker open loop than the poisoning discovery in episode 23.
The wound mystery is answered with Catherine's name; the later poisoning conversation repeats episode 23 with more setup.
The ring-recognition ending is promising, but episode 27 includes the husband and lost-son context inside one clip.
A ring interrogation links her apparently penniless soldier husband to a noblewoman's lost son; cut before his name is spoken.
The accused maid protests innocence; the Duchess confirms she saved her, then breaks off while trying to accuse her attackers.
The gallows threat repeats the captivity premise; episode 12 offers a more concrete choice and episode 34 a judicial deadline.
Manufacturing witchcraft charges is legible but largely explains the villains' plan rather than putting a new viewer inside a dilemma.
The branding threat is graphic and the longer confrontation repeats the worth-and-status argument; stronger alternatives need less context.
The heated-iron ending supplies jeopardy but a standalone cut either repeats insults or depends on the preceding confrontation.
Witness coercion is a viable reserve, but introduces another relationship; the trial itself is clearer for a cold viewer.
The judge offers her a way to save herself; she refuses to condemn healing and he rises to pronounce judgment.
The mother-son reunion resolves recognition; the later ambush account needs more setup than the rescue deadline in episode 36.
An execution threat to his wife becomes a vow that the dead Duke is returning; the rescue and confrontation remain ahead.
Wedding/execution planning is disturbing but mostly exposition; the wife-focused vow in episode 36 supplies the emotional point of view.
The final wedding-bells line needs viewers to know the execution schedule; the bread scene opens gently.
The Duke's transformation is a payoff and preparation montage; the wife's danger is only briefly stated at the end.
Noble arrivals and wedding talk open slowly; the execution threat arrives after substantial scene setup.
The explosion is a strong ending but a 20-60s continuous cut starts in wedding business without clearly explaining the prisoner's danger.
The guards refusing arrest is strong, but the dead-man comeback is substantially answered; episode 43 withholds the betrayers' names.
A royal report establishes a deliberate military leak; cut on the order to read the names, before either conspirator is identified.
Catherine's love appeal resolves in rejection; the unresolved marriage reversal comes in episode 45.
His public declaration makes her a Duchess, then a priest declares her marriage invalid; the reversal leaves her status unresolved.
The ten-day hearing is a usable reserve, but the legal exposition is longer than the immediate reversal in episode 45.
The opening identifies an enemy; the new mistress offers her tormentor shelter only as a scullery maid and demands a choice.
The secret priest summons depends on knowing the hearing, her humiliation and what the priest already did.
A secret priest conspiracy is intriguing, but repeated references to earlier meetings and the council burden standalone clarity.
The priest affair is a scroll hook, but the bargain resolves and the discovery cut needs omitted setup; intimacy also needs footage review.

promos.open_question: How long have her groom and sister been conspiring?
promos.why: The replacement bride declares the betrayal immediately; cut on the unanswered question, before the sister explains how long.
flags: IN: starts within an overlapping visual/audio cue

evidence.text: Close-up on the Lady in Gold Gown beaming with cruel triumph.
"Because he is marrying me."
Close-up on Juliana as tears spill over her eyelashes.
Wide profile shot showing Juliana standing below the altar platform, looking up at Gerald and her sister.
Close-up on Juliana clutching her chest, her sorrow turning into burning outrage.
"You knew this before I walked through those doors!"
Medium shot of Gerald standing stoic and impassive next to the smug Lady in Gold Gown.
Close-up on Juliana's hands desperately clenching fistfuls of her white dress fabric.
"You let me come here..."
Close-up on Juliana's tear-streaked face as she shakes with grief.
"You let me dress in my mother's gown..."
"You let me believe I was walking toward my husband!"
Medium shot on Gerald stepping forward, cold and indifferent, with the Lady in Gold Gown lingering in soft focus behind him.
Tight close-up on Gerald's hardened profile as he glances down.
"I changed my mind."
Extreme close-up on Juliana's furious, weeping face.
"You swore you loved me!"
Close-up on the Lady in Gold Gown smiling condescendingly.
"People change their minds, sister."
Medium profile shot of the Lady in Gold Gown turning her head subtly toward Gerald with satisfied malice.
"And you knew?"
"Of course I knew."
Close-up on Juliana, stunned by the callous depth of the conspiracy.
"How long?"
